speechtext:
It included the ties, I think, but not the rails. The contract went to Mr. Barnes, and, let me say in reference to Mr. Barnes, that he was also a member of the New Brunswick legislature, a member of the Grit machine of the province of New Brunswick, as every member of this directorate was a member of the Liberal machine in that province and he had associated with him in the Barnes Construction *Company the Hon. F. P. Thompson and Mr. W. T. Whitehead and other prominent figures in the Liberal party of the province. They were his chief associates. The commission do not find that Mr. Barnes' associates were advised of the buying off of the lowest tenderer, but if hon. gentlemen will look at the evidence they will find that there is abundant evidence in Mr. Barnes' own statement to justify the finding that these gentlemen were advised of the buying off of the tender of Mr. Wheaton. The upshot was that the contract went to Mr. Barnes for $117,000. What occurred? Last night the Minister of Public Works said that the reason that the contract had been awarded to Mr. Barnes was that he had been such a succes-ful contractor and that Mr. Wheaton had been a failure. The evidence is just to the contrary and the result shows that the minister's statement in regard to Mr. Barnes was absolutely unfounded, because, certainly, if he had never made a failure before, he made a failure of this contract for

he was compelled to throw up the contract in the spring of 1903 and, do you know, that the company actually took that contract off his hands and entered into an arrangement with him for the construction of the road upon a percentage basis agreeing to give him the actual cost of construction plus 15 per cent and that is a way a lot of the grafting was done in connection with this business. I have no hesitation in expressing it as my opinion that the importation of Mr. Barnes into this and the awarding of the contract to Mr. Barnes under these circumstances was with that particular end in view. The Minister of Public Works has spoken about the cost of this fifteen mile section and the unfairness of the commission in allowing only $316,000. Why, Mr. Speaker, that $316,000 is $25,000 more than the Minister of Public Works himself figures in the statement which is on the files. Although the commission express the opinion that this was entirely too much to allow for the construction of that line, they do nevertheless allow the whole amount of $316,000. Mr. Shannon in his report points out that if the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company had done its duty and held Mr. Barnes to his contract the road could have been built for less than $200,000. Mr. Barnes agreed to build his end of it for $117,000 and Mr. Shannon shows that the rails and the engineer's expenses and another item or two would not have amounted to more than $80,000 extra. Furthermore, Mr. Wetmore the provincial engineer was instructed by Provincial Secretary Tweedie to visit the locality and make an examination of the work, and a letter from Mr. Tweedie is on file in which he expresses the greatest dissatisfaction with the manner in which things have been goiilg on. I think it is in reference to this, that the commission used the expression that he had called into play a force which he could not control, and the force which he could not control was the force of the Minister of Public Works. In August, 1903, Mr. Wetmore made a complete report of the value of the work up to that time, and he valued it for the branches and all at $195,000, and that report was sent to Mr. Tweedie. Mr. Tweedie wired Mr. Wetmore for an estimate of what it would cost to complete the road and Mr. Wetmore made another report saying that $31,000 would have completed it. Therefore, on the report of the engineer of the government this road was worth only $226,000. Before the commission evidence was offered as to the cost of similar roads in New Brunswick, and while they have allowed the whole $316,000 it is clear from a perusal of the report that they allowed many thousands of dollars more than was honestly spent in the construction of the railway.
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, I feel Mr. CROCKET.
that I cannot, as a member of the New Brunswick Bar, allow to pass unchallenged the bitter, vindictive and malicious attack which the Minister of Public Works saw fit to make upon an honoured member of the Supreme Court Bench of New Brunswick. I say this, and no one knows it better than the Minister of Public Works, that we have never had upon the Supreme Court Bench of our province-and we have had many eminent judges there-a judge who occupied a higher place in the esteem of the people of the province than does the Hon. Mr. Justice Landry. Not only is Mr. Justice Landry respected and honoured by the people of his own race-and let me say that he is recognized as the most distinguished man the Acadian race has given to the province of New Brunswick-not only is he honoured by the people of his own race and his own creed, But he is honoured by the whole citizenship of New Brunswick irrespective of race and irrespective of creed. And, Sir, it will require far more than the denunciation of the Minister of Public Works to detract from the high reputation which Mr. Justice Landry enjoys, not only in New Brunswick, but throughout this whole Dominion. If there is one quality more than another for which Mr. Justice Landry is distinguished it is his absolute fairness, honesty, and integrity. I repeat that no one knows that better than the Minister of Public Works. I was very much surprised, as a member of this House and as a member of the Bar of New Brunswick, that a gentleman occupying the high position of a minister of the Crown, should make such an unwarranted and malicious attack upon that distinguished citizen of our province. As a member of this parliament and as a member of the Bar, I resent in the strongest possible terms the conduct of the Minister of Public Works in seeking to besmirch the good name of that honoured man. I challenge the Minister of Public Works to point to one single act with which Mr. Justice Landry can be connected either in his public career or his judicial career which does him other than the greatest credit. Mr. Justice Landry was a member of the provincial government of New Brunswick in the days when we had no New Brunswick Coal & Railway frauds. In the regime of that government of which Mr. Justice Landry was a member there was never a single scandal of any discription that could be charged against the administration, and in that government Mr. Justice Landry was the minister of the spending department. I have the feeling that no one will regret more than the Minister of Public Works himself the attack which he was so unwise and so indiscreet as to make in this House last evening upon that honourable and distinguished member of the New

Brunswick judiciary. I do not think that Mr. Justice Landry requires any defence from me. In the documents that I have read to-day and the citations that I have made from the evidence is to be found a vindication of Mr. Justice Landry if vindication were needed. I challenge any member of this House to show wherein the evidence given before that commission does not bear out to the fullest extent every finding made. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but if this commission has erred at all it has erred on the side of leniency.
I have already pointed - out three or four instances in which the name of the Minister of Public Works should have been set forth in the report and where it was omitted, I suppose, out of consideration for the high office he occupies. But if, as the Minister of Public Works said, the commission was actuated only by a reckless desire to destroy him, is it likely that they would have refrained from mentioning his name in reference to some of these transactions where his name is mentioned in the most discreditable manner in the evidence which wras adduced before the commission.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as to the character of this commission, perhaps some members of this House who are not familiar with the public men and with the judges of New Brunswick may take some stock in the statements of the Minister of Public Works, but I can assure them that these the commission, to prove this. The editor pie who live in the maritime provinces. I could quote from an editorial of the St. John ' Globe ' of April 12 last, which refers to these violent attacks made upon the commission to prove this. The editor of the ' Globe, ' is one of the most consistent Liberals in the Dominion, who is one of the most honourable Liberals in the Dominion, and who though possibly he may not be, an intense admirer of the Minister of Public Works, has certainly up to this time enjoyed a good standing in the Liberal party. I could point to this editorial in the St. John 'Globe' to show that it resented these attacks and stated that the commissioners are men of the highest character, as everybody in New Brunswick knows. And, Sir, it will require more than such an attack as was made upon that commission last night to disturb the effect of the findings in that report. I apologize for detaining the House at such great length, but in view of the position which the Minister of Public Works took with regard to the evidence I thought it was necessary. He started out by stating that these findings were not borne out by the evidence and he expressed regret in his own speech and in some of the interruptions during the speech of the hon.
member for West Elgin that the matter was to be confined to a discussion of the report, because what he wanted was the evidence. The Minister of Public Works acknowledged that he had two volumes of the evidence of the witnesses, and there are only two volumes. Yet did he allude to the evidence from the beginning to the end of his five hours' speech yesterday? Not to one syllable, and why? Because he knew that the evidence condemned him more strongly than the report. He made a great talk in the newspapers about the necessity of having the evidence; he admitted yesterday that he had it; but he declined to use it, for the reason I have stated. Now the House has the evidence, and I think I have established by quotations from it that there was not one shadow of justification for the position the Minister of Public Works took in his speech yesterday.
A word or two in reference to a statement that was made by the hon. member for Carleton and also by the Minister of Public Works while the hon. member for West Elgin was speaking yesterday; that was, that they had not had an opportunity of giving evidence, and that the commission had attempted to cut them off. Does my hon. friend from Carleton say that he did not appear as counsel for the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company? Does he say that Mr M. G. Teed did not appear as counsel with him? Does he say that Mr. A. P. Barnhill did not also appear as counsel for the ex-commissioners, Messrs. McAvity and King? I ask the hon. member for Carleton to contrast the conduct of this commission with the conduct of the Insurance Commission which was appointed by this government some years ago, the chief purpose of which I have always thought was to get a crack at the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). An attempt was made to shatter the reputation of the hon. member for North Toronto by the operation of that Insurance Commission. There were charges made of every description. Mr. Foster appeared before that commission, and he was refused again and again the privilege of putting questions through the mouth of his own counsel. And yet a party which issued instructions for the conduct of a commission on such lines as that has the temerity to criticise the conduct of the commission appointed by the New Brunswick government under which the fullest possible opportunity was offered to every counsel who desired to appear on behalf of anybody who had any conceivable interest in the inquiry. I cannot give a better idea of the fairness of Mr. Justice Landry than to quote from pages 61 and 62 of the report of the evidence:

St. John, July 8, 1908.
Commissioners met, pursuant to notice, in the Admiralty Court Room, at 10 a.m., to hear evidence.
The Chairman. This is, virtually the first session of the commission for the particular purpose of taking evidence. It is true, that we met at Fredericton and sat there a short time, but, employed most of the time on the examination of legislation concerning the railway, and in examining certain documents. We called some witnesses, but, inasmuch as this is a public investigation, and as everybody who is interested should have every right to be present, personally, or by counsel, we would like it understood that what we did at Fredericton in the matter of taking evidence is open to the inspection of anybody. The evidence is typewritten, and the witness may be recalled for the purpose of cross-examination or for other purposes.	[DOT]

Teed, K.C., who was present, said: A few moments ago I received a telegram from Mr. F. B. Carvell, at Ottawa, stating that he had been retained to appear for the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company in this investigation, and he wished me to appear to-day and ask for an adjournment. We all know he had his parliamentary duties to attend to, but I am not otherwise aware of the reasons he has for assisting the adjournment. But I should think it would be very important that the company should be represented. I hope your honour may make such an adjournment and allow the hearing to go over until after prorogation of parliament, which, I understand, will be the end of next week.
Mr. Powell. I do not see how this application can bo complied with. It cannot be for the reason of the absence of counsel. There are numerous counsel in the city of St. John who could be engaged. I certainly would oppose a postponement. It does not look like a bona fide application. If there was any real necessity for an adjournment I would consent.
The Chairman. I think we can hardly accede to this request just now, at any rate. I appreciate the interest which this company would have in the proceedings, and perhaps the necessity of their being present-certainly we would be assisted if they were present, but this invstigation is likely to take some little time, and I think it is impossble for us to commence by adjournments to accommodate everybody. If we so commenced we would not know where we would land. Mr. Carvell is employed at Ottawa, and he cannot leave until after adjournment of parliament, the date of which is doubtful. If we were to commence by acceding to all the requests that were made for adjourning, I do not know when we would be liable to close. I think we would meet so as to have the evidence transcribed, and it would be open to these people to have witnesses recalled at any time for the purpose of examination or anything else.
Mr. Teed. Inasmuch as this is the first application on behalf of the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company-while I can understand the force of much Your Honour says -I think in this case they might consider ? prejudiced if not represented.
The Chairman. There is a great deal in what has been said by Mr. Powell that counsel could be obtained. I have had a similar ap-Mr. CROCKET.
plication from the Minister of Public Works, asking an adjournment that he might be present, himself. That letter was written some time ago, and I replied to it, and in his answer he does not insist on an adjournment. If counsel could state a definite time at which he could be present, we would endeavour to accede to his wishes, but, we could hardly adjourn unless there was some fixed date at which we could be assured that the meetings would be held.
After that Judge Landry wrote to the Minister of Public Works as to the importance of his being examined as a witness, and request after request was made by the Minister of Public Works for an adjournment, and his convenience was consulted absolutely. At that very sitting of the commission Mr. Teed appeared as counsel for the company. At the next sitting, in the following week, the hon. member for Carleton appeared as counsel for the company and Mr. A. P. Barnhill appeared as counsel for the ex-commissioners, and on the 20th of August, three months before the Minister of Public Works was examined, he himself appeared as counsel and I happened to be at a session of the commission in which he was conducting an examination of witnesses. In view of this record, it seems to me to have been very bold on the part of the Minister of Public Works to hazard any criticism of the commission in reference to their treatment of the parties and' the privileges of counsel. But could any sane or sensible man be expected to take any stock whatever in the argument that was put up by the Minister of Public Works last night, that he, the managing director of this railway company, who had the responsibility of the company upon him more than any other man, who was familiar with its transactions from beginning to end, who negotiated practically every loan with the banks-that he, having attended the sessions of this commission, having followed,
I assume, as every other citizen did, in the press of New Brunswick, the evidence that was given, would go on the stand in the month of December and not be able to clear up those matters with reference to which there was any doubt. Would anybody believe for one moment that a gentleman of the ability of the Minister of Public Works and of his ingenuity would come forward to give evidence and then simply, because he was not asked a certain question, fail to give any information which would tend to clear up the tangled affairs of the company. But, as a matter of fact, he was asked, as I pointed out by the evidence, what became of the proceeds of the notes which were discounted on the guarantee of these bonds and which he handled, and his evidence speaks for itself. He had no record, no receipts, everything had been handed over to two men, both of whom had

gone to their majority, and he could give the commission no information or enlighten ment. Then he criticised the Attorney General of New Brunswick and the provincial secretary because forsooth they have not been able to supply the evidence which the Minister of Public Works failed to give us regarding his own manipulation of the funds of the company. In view of this evidence, the statement of the Minister of Public Works made yesterday cannot have much weight in the minds of impartial men.
Mr. O'. TURGEON (Gloucester). I have no intention, Mr. Speaker, of following the hon. gentleman who has just addressed the House through the many tortuous windings of the lengthy speech he has made. -When my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. (brothers) brought in a resolution yesterday to the effect that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) should be asked to resign or bo dismissed, he appealed to the very tender regard which the English people have always had for the character of their public men, and he hoped that the high record they had shown in that respect would not be departed from in this instance in Canadian public life. With that sentiment, I am in perfect harmony with my hon. friend and so is every true Canadian who has the honour at heart of the men to whose guidance are entrusted the destinies of this great nation. But because we are jealous of the character of our public men is no reason why we should fall into the opposite extreme and create bad impressions, not only among our own people, but in countries outside of Canada, regarding the conditions of Canadian public life. The time has come, it seems to me, when we ought to cry halt in our endeavour to achieve political success by suspecting scandals where they do not exist. Changes of government have taken place before this session. We have had recently a change of government in New Brunswick. A few years ago we had a change of government in Ontario, when the party which had held the reins of power for many years was compelled to give place to its opponent. Inquiries of all kinds have been made, commissions appointed and changes have also taken place in other provinces, but are we to expect that whenever there is a change of government, its successors must appoint commissions to find out evils in the administrations of its predecessors, and have those reports brought before the federal Parliament, as in this case, which aire foreign to our jurisdiction. My hon. friend from Elgin, to add to the solemnity of his language, made several times the declaration that he was standing for the report of a judicial commission. Well, for my part, every time I took up the report of
this judicial commission, I found it impossible, according to my own conscience and my own intelligence to reconcile my judgment with every assertion made in that report.
Fearing, perhaps, that if the name of Judge Landry did not appear at the head of that commission, there would be less respect for its findings, my hon. friend from York county made a reference to the standing of Judge Landry before the bar and the people of New Brunswick and the people of the Acadian race whose interests he has advocated so ably on so many different occasions. Well, no man in this House could have a greater respect for Judge Landry than the member for Gloucester who is now addressing you. One of my proudest recollections is to have had the good fortune, in the starting years of my public life, to have had the honour of collaborating with him in his endeavour to bring the Acadian race, by means of education to the level of the other races.
Meanwhile my respect for Judge Landry, the respect in which he is held in the province of New Brunswick and which he specially enjoys as a judge of the Supreme Court of that province, does not grant him the gift of infallibility, and his judgment with that of the other commissioners, of whom my hon. friend has spoken so highly is not necessarily to be accepted without question. When I study this report of the commission, I find myself at times unable to find'in it any evidences of the judicial attitude. I am not a lawyer or, as the saying is, the son of a lawyer-I am only the father of a lawyer;-but I appeal to every man of legal training and legal ability in this House to say if he can find in this report the judicial tone which the hon. member for west Elgin (Mr. Crothers) has endeavoured to make the House believe it had and because of which, apparently, he sought to invest it with infallibility. When I look at this document, I fail to recognize the wisdom, the lucid explanation of legal matters characteristic of my old friend Judge Landry and shown by him on many a previous occasion. I fail to see the evidences of careful thought in this Teport. I wholly fail to appreciate the conclusions resting upon assumptions which, at times, can hardly be said to be sound. I find in some of the conclusions of this report rather the characteristics of a political harangue by a stump speaker, regardless of the responsibility of his utterances. There are only a couple of points to which I wish to call attention, and which particularly struck me from the first. These points I cannot explain to myself; I believe they are enough to cast suspicion on the judicial findings of this report based upon evidence which is not at our command to-day, we are here called upon to pass judgment upon the

political life of one of the biggest men, to use the expression of my hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket), whom the province of New Brunswick has ever produced. We are called upon to eliminate from public life a man who has been at the head of affairs in his own province, and who in this parliament has taken a foremost place and since he has been amongst us has commanded the sympathy and admiration of every hon. member. And why should we be called upon to discuss this report? The legislature to which it belongs has not seen fit to discuss it. This report was placed upon the table of the House of Assembly of the province of New Brunswick, and for thirty days thereafter that House was in session, and no action was taken, or attempted to be taken, upon the report. What is the reason that the present leader -the temporary leader I may say-of that House did not see fit to call the attention of the legislature to this report and ask the legislature to review it? But we, the great parliament of Canada, are called upon to discuss a question beyond our sphere and foreign to our duty while the legislature of New Brunswick for whose benefit this report is made, has left the discussion of it over for another year at least.
One of the first points to which I wish to call the attention of this parliament is to be found in the second paragraph of the conclusion of the report. It may be said again that I am appealing to that figure which is called a typographical error. In saying that $430,000 and $500,000 are misprints here for $43,000 and $50,000. But leave out the possibility of a typographical error, and I ask you again, if these commissioners were really alive to the responsibilities of their actions and findings, could it be possible for such an error to be allowed to pass?
On the face of it the motive of the promoters as stated was to develop the coal mines of Queens county. Responsible and respectable men from various parts of the province were obtained to lend their names as directors; and from the fact that $430,000 of the total $500,000 authorized capital was to be distributed as founders' shares, we conclude that the interested parties had visions of ultimate large profits, with absolute certainty of no personal loss.
If this was a typographical error, if the commissioners had in view merely the sum of $43,000, then there was no reason for 'visions of ultimate large profits with absolute certainty of no personal loss,' and therefore these words should not have been used in this report. Another point to which I wish to call attention is the great difference in the conditions of railway building as they exist now and existed twenty or thirty years ago. It strikes me that if I were called upon to require an estimate for the construction of a railroad Mr. TURGEON.
I would apply to engineers with experience in railroad construction; I would not be simply guided by the estimates which may have been given by engineers twenty or thirty years before the date of the construction of this 15-mile section, and conclude that because a few miles of railroad may have been built in the early days in New Brunswick for $10,000 a mile or less, to-day you can build in other sections of the province a railway for a somewhat similar amount or double the amount. We must remember that conditions of railway building have changed completely, in the cost of labour, in the cost of materials, and in every other way. There can be no possible comparison between the cost of railway building in the two periods. Thirty years ago you could get labour for the asking. I knew men in those days working on railroads in my own county for 75 and 80 cents a day, and they were paid out of the stores of the contractors whatever price the contractors chose to ask for their goods. In those days railway ties could be bought for a few cents apiece. I have the testimony of my hon. friend from Kent county who, in his early years, sold railway ties for 15, 13 and 12 cents apiece. Now I ask vou, Mr. Speaker, how much has the present Minister of Public Works or his predecessor had to pay for railway ties? Why, Sir, the prosperity of Canada has advanced the value of every possible commodity. I am safe in saying that in Kent county to-day it costs 200 per cent more to construct a railway than it did in the former period. It is also to be remembered that modern railways are much more solidly built, they are built for the purpose of transporting coal and heavy freight, whereas in former days they were built for the transportation of a few boxes of fish and a few passengers. And because this railroad has cost 100 per cent more than our friends think it should have cost, they say there has been a misappropriation of $242,000 upon that section. I say, Mr. Speaker, that such a conclusion lends itself to doubt and suspicion on the part of every honest man who wishes to come to a correct conclusion. These two points are sufficient, I think, to answer the contentions of our hon. friend opposite. It is not my intention to follow in detail the long speech of the hon. member for York, N.B. (Mr. Crocket). It was not my purpose in rising to defend the hon. the Minister of Public Works. That hon. gentleman has proved on many occasions that he is quite able to defend himself; he has proved it twice already during the present session; he proved abundantly last night that he needs no one to come to his defence when he is attacked, that he is w'ell able to stand against the calumnies of his political op-

ponents. I may say that since this debate was begun yesterday I have had some conversation with hon. members, both of this House and of the Senate, and they are by no means in sympathy with the motion of censure. I am confident that this motion does not meet with the approval of every Conservative in the Dominion of Canada, nor even of every Conservative member in this House. I am sure that the Minister of Public Works yesterday satisfied every member in this House who desires to form an impartial judgment, that as ex-officio director of this company he knew everything that wras being done; and if at one time when he had to take over this road it was found that the company had got into financial difficulties, I say it is no new thing in our province of New Brunswick. We have found in the past that when our public men were endeavouring to develop the great resources of our country they did not meet with the encouragement they were entitled to. Today we are doing everything possible to develop the west, knowing that its development will mean the progress of the east. I think that when our public men enter into schemes for the development of our province of New Brunswick, and of the Dominion of Canada, they are deserving of more encouragement than they receive That has been a trouble that has existed in the past. I hope that after all, when this matter has been thoroughly sifted, when the judgment of this parliament and of the country has been pronounced, it will be that these men who were acting in the interest of the province are deserving of more encouragement than they had received. Hon. gentlemen opposite contend that $20,000 a mile should have been sufficient to build that railway. What did we find in the legislature of New Brunswick when that very report was laid upon the table of the legislature of the local legislature?
Only two weeks ago, and since that report has been placed upon the table of the House, Premier Hazen, the leader of the government, has undertaken to give the guarantee of the province of New Brunswick for a railway with the same objects as this one	had,	that	is for the	development of an iron mine, for a railway which	traverses	the county	ofGloucester from Nipisiquit river to Bathurst, and which will assist in the development of the iron ore deposits there. He does not estimate the cost of the railway construction in New Brunswick at $5,000 or $10,000 but he gives a guarantee of $15,000 a	mile	and	this when	heknows' that	the	very	same company
are also applying to this government for a subsidy of $6,400 a mile. The fact that he is willing to give the guarantee of
his province to the extent of $15,000 a mile is an admission that railway construction in New Brunswick cannot be carried on for $8,000 or $11,000 or even for $20,000 a mile. Therefore, his action, patriotic as it may be, in giving this guarantee, which I approve of, and I have advised his supporters to second his efforts in this matter, is a contradiction of the finding of this commission as to the cost of railway construction in New Brunswick. In conclusion, I wish again to say that, whatever the vote upon the opposition side of the House may be, we, on this side of the House, feel convinced of the moral innocence of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. He has devoted a lifetime to the public affairs of the province of New Brunswick and in every sphere into which his activities have entered he has won a high place in _ the affection and esteem of patriotic Canadians in all parts of the Dominion who have observed his public conduct. To-day every Liberal in the province of New Brunswick, every unbiased man, to whatever party he may belong, feels, as my right hon. friend the Prime Minister said a few days ago that he felt, proud of the Minister of Public Works. Every friend of ours in the province of New Brunswick is satisfied that the Minister of Public Works has faithfully discharged the trust which was reposed in him when he was called to the federal arena to give his important services, not only to the great Liberal party to which he belongs, but to the Dominion at large. I shall consider it my duty to vote against the resolution and I feel that in doing so I shall have the confidence and support -of all of my constituents in the county of Gloucester. I feel also that I shall have the sympathy and support of the great Acadian race in the province of New Brunswick, of which the hon. member for York has spoken, which has shown its appreciation of the development of the resources of this country under a Liberal government for the last thirteen years and which has no ground to alter its views with regard to any public man because of anything contained in the report of this

Because its provincial government does so much on these lines that there is no demand for us to do that kind of work. The work is done and the farmers are receiving the benefit and we are able to economize in that province. In Quebec about $2,500. That is partly to help the live stock association. It is unfortunate perhaps that there are in Quebec associations which are not affiliated to the General Dominion Association. Still they are doing good work in their own province; and if they were not kept up, there would be a very serious damage to a very important industry in that province. I am obliged to give them assistance to the extent of $600. We have also taken upon ourselves to do a good deal more in the way of institute work in the province of Quebec among the French Canadian farmers because the provincial government does not do as much and here is a great demand for assistance and addresses. We are therefore spending a larger amount there than in the other provinces, where a great deal of that kind of work is done by the provincial authorities, and the language being different makes the cost a little more. In New Brunswick, $1,000; in Nova Scotia, $1,100. We give to the Maritime Special Breeders' Association, which holds a winter fair in Amherst, New Brunswick, assistance to the extent of a little over $2,500. Then we have a special work for the encouragement of what is called a record of performance among dairy stock. This was inaugurated two years ago by my department to encourage the breeders of thoroughbred dairy cows to test their animals and establish a record of performance. That is a very useful work. The stock breeders have taken advantage of it very greatly and we have been obliged to increase the expenditure. To-day we have three men, whose whole time is taken up by it. It is a work which requires a government official so as to insure absolute confidence in the test. We began with only one man but we had so many demands for the test that we had to add another. A third has to be added and I think shortly more still. This shows that the people are taking an interest in the work and that it is effective. We also publish reports of the live stock branch and have some general expenses for travelling and office expenses, and we also deal in this branch with what are called national live stock records. A few years ago there were thoroughbred records of the different kinds of animals in the different provinces, and my department undertook, after discussions with the different breeders of thoroughbred live stock, to establish national records. To-day we have national records, recognized, not only all Mr. FISHER.
over Canada but outside of Canada, as absolutely trustworthy and these certificates are received in foreign countries with confidence. That costs about $10,000 a year. We also do a little in the way of developing and encouraging the sale of thoroughbred stock from one province to another. In the old days the only good market, if not the only market, for the thoroughbred breeders in Ontario was in the United States. There was a great demand for thoroughbred stock in the west and the east when my department undertook to bring together the purchasers and sellers and give them facilities for the transfer of stock. That takes $1,500 or $1,600. We have besides a general representative in Manitoba and the west, whose salary and office expenses come to about $1,600. I wish that time would allow me to give a more complete description of the work, because I am rather proud of it, and I think it is doing good for our farmers and live stock breeders.

Has the Minister of Agriculture had any communication from the live stock association of Manitoba asking for assistance to ship their- stock to the exhibition at Seattle during the coming summer? I have had a letter from the association which I presume the minister has received also and therefore shall not read it. We have not bothered the minister much during the session, but those interested in agriculture think that this great industry is not getting the consideration it ought, and I regret very much that the hon. minister held up his estimates as usual to this late hour. I believe the minister (Mr. Fisher), from the way he looks at me at this moment is in a better humour than he was just before six o'clock when he took his hat and hurriedly left the building. I am glad that he has come back and that he appears to foe in as philosophical a state of mind as he does to-night. I hope he will use his influence to get for the agriculturists of this country a due proportion of the appropriations for the development of their great industry. On a previous occasion this session, I accused the minister of sitting back quietly and allowing other ministers to dip their hands into the treasury and get large appropriations for their departments, while the Department of Agriculture was allowed to suffer. I have pointed out to him, and I would do the same to-night, that nearly all the money that is paid into the treasury comes from the farmers of this country, and yet they are not getting the consideration they are entitled to. I hope the minister will see his way to granting to the agricultural associations of Manitoba the small request they make for an appropriation of $7,500 to enable them to take their stock to this great exhibition which is to take place in the near future. It would be a great boon not only to the prairie provinces but to the whole of Canada. No doubt, the minister will answer that these appropriations must be made from the federal standpoint and that Manitoba stands in the same position as other provinces in relation to such claims as this. But I think he will appreciate the fact that, owing to the agricultural situation of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, they have not been able to take advantage of the appropriations made to them on previous occasions to assist exhibitors to the same degree as other provinces lying close to where these exhibitions have

My hon. friend (Mr. Staples) seems to think that I was not in a good humour this afternoon. I was in a very good humour; I was out at the Experimental Farm where I like to be. I left the House under the impression that hon. members were going to continue the debate for some time; I was told, in fact, that it might continue until two or three o'clock in the morning. When I came back, I was surprised, and, I confess, pleased, to find that the question was closed, and that something else might be taken up. I am consequently in a very good humour because this debate is closed and we are able to go on with the proper work of the session, instead of it being interrupted in the way it has been. The hon. gentleman advises me to get larger appropriations for the benefit of the farmers. I know that hon. gentlemen opposite often suggest individual increases of expenditure; but, unfortunately, the sum total has to be considered, and the same hon. gentlemen object very much to the increase there. But individual items cannot be increased without increasing the sum total. Therefore, I have to Tegard the treasury of the country and the criticisms which are levelled at the government as a whole and try to keep the sum total down as low as I can. If I am successful in doing that, my hon. friends must not criticise me' too hard for my success in economy. At the same time, I think I have shown that I do not hesitate to ask for money for agricultural expenditure when necessary, and when I can see my way clear to spend it foT the real advantage of the farmers. The increase in the agricultural expenditure, which is so great, is the evidence of what I have done. The hon. member asked me with regard to communication from the live stock men of Manitoba regarding live stock exhibits at Seattle. I shall have to answer the hon. gentleman much as I did the secretary of the association. It has been known for a long time that Canada was going to exhibit at Seattle-the announcement was made long ago. All preparations for this exhibit were made four or five months ago. Money was put into the estimates for this exhibition, and the money was allotted to the different parts of the work in connection with it. It is only within the last few weeks that the Manitoba farmers have waked up, apparently, and the request has been forwarded to me by the secretary of the association. As I have said, all the money voted for the exhibition has been allotted, and there is none available for the exhibit of live stock. I must say, however, that I do not consider that a matter to cause us very deep regret.

Why? For two reasons: In the first place, the quarantine arrangements on the United States border are such that the sending of live stock to the exhibition at Seattle would be almost impossible. I do not think any live stock owners in Canada would care to undergo the restrictons which the quarantine regulations of the United States impose on them in sending their live stock to Seattle. Hon. gentlemen may say that these quarantine regulations may be suspended or some modification of them may be reached. Well, I have information that the authorities of that exhibition have been trying to secure a suspension of the regulations or some modification of them, and have failed.

Ryan of Montreal with reference to disseminating through the Dominion certain thoroughbred stock, stallions for breeding purposes. The minister knows that we had Mr. Ryan up here after the convention a short time' ago, and the minister said he would take a little time to consider the request which was made by Mr. Ryan's company. I would like to know what conclusion he has come to. subtopic: MEMORANDUM FOR BONDS SIGNED AND DELIVERED LATER.
speechtext:
My hon. friend I think was present when I received Mr. Ryan and some of his friends regarding that matter of breeding. The proposition was one which sounded very attractive, and I can understand how attractive it would appear to many farmers throughout the country who would keep the stallions and take the fees which would be paid for their service. I was not at all surprised that a large number of petitions in favour of the proposition were signed by people all over the country._ But I myself looked upon the proposition with a little suspicion because of its very attractiveness and apparent lack of reason why a group of gentlemen should make such an offer. However, I received the deputation along with several gentlemen of the House, and we had a little discussion on it. As a result, I asked Mr. Ryan to make me a definite proposition. .The proposition which he submitted at that time was one for an assistance of $50,000 to be paid to the National Bureau cf Breeding, in consideration of their dis-

tributing 100 thoroughbred stallions in Canada, in other words, at the rate of $500 a horse, they to provide the animals and look after them. I asked Mr. Ryan why he needed that assistance. He had stated to us that he got the horses for little or nothing, and he did not want consideration for the price of the horses. I asked him, therefore, to submit to me a scheme in detail, and he did submit a scheme on a smaller scale, asking for $25,000 a year subsidy for this particular association, in consideration of providing 50 thoroughbred stallions to be distributed over the country, and to be put into the hands of the farmers who would receive the fees, and they would charge $10 a service for the horses. I asked why they needed this $25,000 from the government. He submitted .to me a scheme of their expenses. When I came to examine that scheme I found it on so large a scale that I thought I could understand the proposition. I knew perfectly well that through the officers of my department and through the machinery which I had, all the work Mr. Ryan and his friends were proposing to do for $25,000 a year, could be done for about one-third or less by the department. I was not prepared therefore to pay that liberal subsidy for this purpose.
But I found other difficulties. This was a scheme for the purpose of spreading English thoroughbred blood in the country. Now, no man in Canada is more appreciative of the value of English thoroughbred blood among the horses of Canada than myself. I think it would be a very good thing indeed to get a considerable infusion of that blood into the horseflesh of the country, and I would do a good deal to accomplish that. At the same time I cannot help remembering, as a minister, that if the country subsidizes thoroughbred stallions we are creating a keen competition to the owners of other stallions in Canada, that the owners of hackneys, the standard breed horses and others of the lighter kind, would be injured by such subsidizing of the English thoroughbred stock; and if they felt so injured, they would be perfectly justified, and I might expect they would ask me to do just as much on behalf of the other breeds. I realized that such an arrangement as this for the propagation of English thoroughbred stock in Canada would necessarily and legitimately lead to the calling for a similar expenditure on behalf of the hackney horses, and on behalf of the standard bred horses, and perhaps some other breeds, and I could not see my way to recommend to parliament an expenditure of this character. Some people may say that it would not interfere with the other horses. But it stands to reason that if to-day, in
a particular neighbourhood, there is a pure bred hackney stallion and no other pure bred stallion, and you subsidize a pure bred English stallion, he would certainly take away some of the custom of the hackney stallions, and the hackney breeders would be justified in saying that the country's money was being used to hurt them; and if that money was paid out for the one class of stock it ought to be paid out for the others, and I would not be able to answer their objection. Under these circumstances I could not see my way to accepting the proposition that was made, and I wrote to Mr. Ryan saying that I could not entertain his proposition.

speechtext: I will take this opportunity to direct the minister's attention to the hog raising industry in Canada, which, I think, would properly come under this item. My hon. friend is the master of the agriculture interests of Canada

speechtext:
Well, we do not always think that he is the servant. Sometimes he is the master. I had the opportunity of presenting some very important figures to the House during a former discussion this session as to the condition of the hog raising industry. My hon. friend had before him a deputation of the Swinebreeders' Association of Canada complaining of the condition of the hog trade and pointing out that while there was a large importation of hogs into Canada a very small amount of hog products were exported to the United States. They also brought the condition of the tariff to his attention. The tariff rate on hogs coming into Canada is two cents a pound, while the United States tariff rate is five cents a pound. Last year we inported over $1,000,000 worth more than we exported and it seems to me that this would be a legitimate question for my hon. friend to turn his attention to. When the Swinebreeders' Assocation, representing the farmers of this country, point out that the condition of the hog industry is such that it requires special protection this government should devote some attention to it. It may be that it would require ' Mr. BARR.
a sum to be placed in the estimates to make a complete examination into the condition of the trade in Canada. Perhaps my hon. friend could take some portion of this money and devote to it. We have some converts on the subject and if my hon. friend will not listen to myself or to any hon. gentleman on this side of the House he may listen to some of his own friends. This session we have the hon. member for Wentworth (Mrj. 'Sealey) and the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Schell) as converts to the idea of affording protection to the swine industry of Canada. The hon. member for Wentworth, in the early part of the session, placed a resolution on the Order Paper calling upon this government to increase the duty on hog products. My hon. friend, of course, withdrew it, but he ventured to suggest to the government that it was the duty of the government to comply with the request of the Swinebreeders' Association and he was endorsed by the hon. member who represents South Oxford, also a supporter of the government. My hon. friend is asking the committee to vote a considerable sum of money for the improvement of the stock industry in Canada. While my hon. friend is a supporter of a government that is supposed to be giving some protection to the industries of the country, I hope he will not forget the farmers. My hon. friend has an opportunity now to do something for the farmers by complying with the request of the Swinebreeders' Association and it seems to me that it would be an opportune time to place, a sum in the estimates, or see that some portion of this money is used to make a thorough investigation of the hog industry so that the government will know whether it is in the best interests of Canada that a higher protection should be placed upon hog products. My hon. friend had a special opportunity during last year. We had a great presidential election in the United States in which the tariff question occupied a foremost nlace. My hon. friend has treated this House in days gone by to statements of what he was able to do with the United States government. This ought to be an opportune time for the Minister of Agriculture to use his influence with the United States government, and if he is not able to persuade his own government to increase the duty on pork to four cents a pound perhaps he may be able to persuade the United States government to decrease their duty on pork so that the farmers of Canada might have an equal opportunity with the farmers of the United States to share in the growth of this industry. I suppose the minister will have to tell the committee that he has naid no attention to the revision of the tariff in the United States. When he was in opposition he told us that it would only take a moment

to open the United States market to the farmers of Canada, but probably he has not lately been reading ancient history. My hon. friend shakes his head at that, but I would impress upon him that it will not do for this government to profess that they are the friends of the farmers when they turn deaf ears to deputations of farmers who come to them, and when they refuse the demands of their own supporters in this House that the farmers be given equal justice under the tariff. If my hon. friend does not prove his _own statement that he is the greatest friend of the farmers, then the farmers must turn a deaf ear to the hon. gentleman when he comes to Halton and other places and tells them of all he has been doing for them. Let the Minister of Agriculture tell us now whether he intends to do anything for the farmers in connection with the hog raising industry, and whether he will expend some of this vote in finding out whether the Swinebreeders' Association were right when they told the government that the Canadian market is being flooded with pork from the United States. These gentlemen did not ask that the duty on pork should be five cents a pound as it is in the United States, our own tariff being two cents, but they made the humble request that the Canadian duty shall be four cents. I am surprised that the Minister of Agriculture has nothing in the estimates for the purpose of helping this industry and that he has no comforting assurance to give now to the farmers of Canada.

speechtext:
My hon. friend says 'quite right.' He seems to be of the opinion that it is well if possible to raise prejudices between the different classes and the people who are engaged in the different industries in the country. To me that is

not the proper statesmanship to apply to the solution of difficult questions. I think that if a remedy can he found for any particular industry which will not hurt any body else, it is much better than to adopt a remedy which does hurt other people. My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) says that higher protection would be the panacea, but I tell him frankly that I do not agree with him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
subtopic: MEMORANDUM FOR BONDS SIGNED AND DELIVERED LATER.
speechtext: Then my hon. friend differs from the farmers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
subtopic: MEMORANDUM FOR BONDS SIGNED AND DELIVERED LATER.
speechtext:
I do sometimes. There are farmers and farmers; there are some farmers who think one thing and there are some farmers who think another thing, and I thank God that in Canada all the farmers as a class do not set their interests against the interests of other people in the community, but believe that the industrial classes and the consuming classes as well as the farmers have to be considerd in dealing with such questions. I am glad that I belong to the class that thinks that way and acts that way in the public interests. My hon. friend seems to think that is the only remedy-higher protection. It matters not whom it hits or how much it hits the rest of the community. That I do not consider to be true national policy or true statesmanship. I think it is well that any class in the community should be helped and that in helping that class we should at the same time help the rest of the community. The farmers of Canada have generally condemned the policy of exclusive protection for a few people at election after election. My hon. friend knows well that when this government brought down their tariff, the essence of which is not protection, he and his friends allowed it to be passed without daring to put themselves on record by challenging a vote of the House on a single item. Did my hon. friend and his friend two weeks ago, when the Finance Minister brought down his tariff, move for any changes in it ? No. They allowed it to he passed unanimously by this House, and it has gone out not only to this country but to the world that the Fielding tariff is the best tariff Canada has ever had, and I venture to think that in the future as in the past the electors of Canada, especially the farmers, will support the government which brought that tariff down and put it on the statute book of this country. My hon. friend talks about the swine-breeders. I am ready to help the swine-breeders, very ready. They are an intelligent people; they have been doing good things not only for the swine-breeders of Canada, but for the people of Canada at large. It has been only since the first tariff of Mr. Fielding was brought down in 1896 that the j bacon industry of Canada has grown J Mr. FISHER.
to any appreciable extent; and it is through the information that has been spread abroad through the country to a large extent that the swine-breeders of Canada have been able to produce in the last ten years over $100,000,000 of swine products for export. I am ready to go further and continue that policy of education and information, which helps not only the people concerned, but everybody in the country. I do not wish to raise the price of the pork which the labouring classes of this oountry have to buy. I wish to help the farmers of the country to produce the pork so that they can sell it at present prices and make a splendid profit on those prices.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
subtopic: MEMORANDUM FOR BONDS SIGNED AND DELIVERED LATER.
speechtext:
No. I wish to continue my argument unbroken, and my hon. friend can argue against me when I am done. I believe that the best profits in every industry are made by cheapening the cost of production rather than by raising the cost of the article. When you raise the cost of the article, you hurt the consumer of the article, though you may possibly for the moment increase the profits of the producer, but when you lower the cost of production, you give the producer his profits without raising the cost to the consumer, and therefore the consumer is not hurt. In this particular industry of swine breeding and pork production our greatest rivals are the Danes and the Irish. They have beaten us in the English market in tire sale of pork products. Now, instead of raising the prices of pork products to the people of Canada, who have to buy them, I want to find out how the Danes and the Irish succeed in beating our people in the British market, and for that purpose I have asked and have obtained permission from my colleagues to bring down a vote in the supplementary estimates for the purpose of sending a special commission of farmers interested in the swine breeding industry of Canada, to Ireland and Denmark to investigate the methods of production in those countries. My hon. friend seems to think that I am not taking care of the interests of the swine breeders in Canada because we do not bring down a higher tariff. I believe I am doing what is better-better for the swine breeders themselves, and certainly better for the whole consuming public of Canada; and I believe it is better than my hon. friend's sole panacea for all the commercial troubles of the country-higher and higher protection. My hon. friend alluded to the United States elections. I watched those elections with interest, because anything that goes on in the United States is of interest to us in Canada, and also because conditions in the United States are similar to conditions in

this country. If my hon. friend had watched those elections closely, he would have seen that the tariff was one of the most important issues, and he would have seen lately that President Taft declared that he was elected in November last to revise the tariff downwards and not upwards, not to increase protection, l?ut to decrease protection. If there is any lesson to be learned from the success of the Republican party in the last elections, it is that even that party, rabid and extreme protectionists as they are, were obliged to promise the electors that they would reduce their tariff and not increase it. If this is the case, the idea that my hon. friend brings forward, that we must remedy all our evils in this country by raising our tariff higher and higher on everything, is not following the example of the United States, but is something quite different; and I believe that what I am prepared to do for the swine breeders of Canada is more in their interest, more in the interest of consumers. and better altogether for the country. I am prepared to do that. I have not ignored their demands. One of their demands was that a commission should be sent to Denmark and Ireland, and I am glad to be able to say to the House and the country that the government are going to bring down an estimate for that purpose, and I trust that hon. gentlemen opposite, who are so solicitous at the moment for the interests of the swine breeders, will assist us in passing that item unanimously.

speechtext:
It is rather surprising to me that under an item in the estimates we should branch off on a discussion of the tariff; but as the Minister of Agriculture has set us such a good example, perhaps we had better deal with that question for a while. The hon. gentleman's policy, I admit, is a policy of importation, as against the old Ipolicy of production, which existed prior to his coming into office. The tariff of the Liberal-Conservative government was framed to produce all we could in Canada, but the hon. gentleman seems to think that the proper poliey is to promote importation. Now, I am not going to advocate any increased protection. I do not need to do so, because the hon. Minister of Agriculture and his associates have done that for me. I do not know that we have ever had a higher protectionist government in power in Canada since 1878 than we have to-day. I had occasion a short time ago to enumerate a number of articles-and I gave only a very few, though I might have gone on by the half hour enumerating article after article-on which they raised the tariff away and beyond what the Conservative party ever thought of. What induced the hon. gentleman to agree two years ago that a woman's shoe should be raised from 25 to 30 per cent, and how can he say he
is a free trader or a low tariff man? Why does he tax the women on their shoes? Is it because he himself has no women to look after? Even if he has not, he ought to have some regard for those who have. He ought to have some regard for those who have wives and daughters. But he says: ' Let the women pay the duty; a tariff for revenue only is what I want.' All he thinks of is the money. On ladies' furs, cloaks, muffs and tippets he has increased the duty from 25 to 30 per cent, and then he tells us he is a low tariff man; but if raising the tariff makes him a low tariff man, the hon. gentleman must be in a class by himself. Even the porridge we get for breakfast had to be increased in duty in order to satisfy his low tariff proclivities; and now he wants to make us believe that if we have a higher tariff on pork products, that will increase the price to the consumer, and he says he is looking after the consumer. Let me tell him that if we can increase the raising of hogs and their products in this country, we will do more to cheapen the market for the consumer than anything else we can do. But so long as you permit hog products to come in and invade our market in such a way that our producers are driven out of business, our consumers will have to pay high prices for these products. I have a statement here prepared by officers of the hon. minister's own government-men who speak with authority. Do they say that food products are cheaper to-day than they were under the Conservative regime? Quite the reverse. Let me give a few illustrations. Fresh meat and bacon, they say, have increased 45 to 50 per cent the last ten years; bacon has advanced 45 per cent; beef, 50 per cent; veal, 57 per cent; mutton, 55 per cent. Does this show the hon. gentleman has done anything for the consumer? Has he done anything for the producer? We are not producing the quantity of hogs and bacon that we did many years ago. By promoting a policy of importation, the hon. gentleman, instead of causing a large number of hogs to be raised and a larger quantity of bacon to be supplied, has reduced the production. But what does he care so long as he gets a revenue? Promote importation, kill off the industries of the country if you can, never mind the farmer. The hon. gentleman was kind enough to come to my county during the last election and make a strong appeal to the electors to reject me, who, though not a farmer myself, have always advocated the interests of the farmers, who has always stood by them in advocating protection of their fruits and their grains and in urging the adoption of a farmers' policy all along the line. The hon. minister went all the way to a town in the heart of my

county to address a mass meeting. About 400 were present, 200 of whom were Conservatives who went out of curiosity to see what kind of a man that was who would advise them to take a man from Toronto who knew nothing about farming and elect him as their representative instead of one who for 20 odd years had advocated their interests. Not only did he do that, but he went to South Ontario and opposed the late representative of that county, a representative live stock man, and urged the people to turn him down and put in a man who had no claim to represent them in parliament. 1 am not finding fault with the hon. minister for having done that, but if he has no sympathy with the farmers, why does he not say so? He went to East Elgin and endeavoured to defeat a gen, tleman who was aiding the farmers by buying their products as largely as any man in this country. His policy is importation. Get your hog products, bacon and hams and pork from the United States, if you do not import these things, we will get no revenue. That is his policy. What he is looking after is customs revenue, and he has no care for the farmers. We do not want class legislation, he says, which will help one class and hurt another. Well, I undertake to say that legislation which will help the farmer will help the business man. The more you reduce the amount of pork produced in this country the higher the price. That is fully born out by this statement prepared by officers of the government.

It is a statement prepared by the civil servants, officers of this government. It is thoroughly authentic. The hon. minister based his Civil Service Bill on it. I think the minister had better just make up his mind that the farmers have some rights and that it is not for him to cry them down on every occasion and say that they come to him as a class and want something for themselves which will hurt others. I do not think that this will hurt others. Let him give a little consideration to the swine breeders.
I do not know what their requests are. I am not going to tell him what he should do, but I think something should be done. He complained in Halton that I had advocated a higher tariff on hog products. Well, what do you think the people said? They said, 'He is the man we want, we will stick to him ' and they elected me by a larger majority than ever. The minister had better take warning. The farmers know what they want and are not going to be turned away by any such representation.
I am convinced that a tariff which would Mr. HENDERSON.
give _ a little better encouragement to the hog industry would be a very good thing. But that- question is not before us now, and I am not here to advocate it to-night. I would be glad, however, to .see that done. My impression is that it would increase the production of hogs and their products, and if you could increase that- production by 25 per cent that would reduce the price to the consumer; and instead of having bacons and hams increase 45 to 50 per cent over what they sold at ten years ago, the consumer would get them at a lower price. If the farmer could sell twice as much hog products, he would make more. Now he is not carrying on the business to. the same extent simnly because he does not find it remunerative.
Now, the minister has my ideas on that question. But I do not think he has any reasons to cast reflections upon the farmers and to say they want class legislation. They are a class and a large class, and they have just as good a right to have their class considered as any other in the community. I think anything that will help the farmers will help every other class, the manufacturers, business men, private individuals and even the gentlemen who prepared this* document, for I believe it will be the means of increasing the supplies in the market and so lowering the price,-it will be better for all classes. In considering the live stock industry along these lines, the minister will be doing more for the farmers and all other classes.

speechtext:
I did not suppose for a moment, when I ventured to direct the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) to the condition of the hog industry that he would altogether lose his head in this discussion. He has branched out into the whole tariff question in Canada, as he is quite willing to do sometimes; and, if the time of this House is being taken up, at this late date of the session, with a discussion of this kind, the hon. gentleman must be held responsible for it. I was clearly within my right when I undertook, on an agricultural item to direct attention to one specific industry, and if my hon. friend had dwelt upon this for half an hour as he has, dealing with the whole tariff question, it is a matter for himself and the House to consider and one for which I am not responsible, and no man within the sound of my voice would venture to hold me responsible for the course the discussion has taken. I am sure the farmers would have been very pleased if the minister had been as frank with the deputation that came to see him and his government as he has been with this committee. He says that the farmers want special legislation for themselves. He had not the courage, when the farmers' deputation met him a few weeks ago, to tell them, as he did this committee, that he was opposed to an increase of the duty on pork. Will he venture to say that he'did? He has views and opinions on this question, he says. But he would allow the farmers to come down, as he did a few weeks ago, and meet him and his government with their specific request, a request which has been read in this House by one or two of his own supporters, a request for an increase in the duty on pork coming into Canada. They pointed out to him and his government that the duty on pork coming into Canada was two cents per lb. while the duty on pork going into the United States was five cents per lb. The farmers pointed out that this was unfair to their interest as between 85,000,000 of people on one side and 7,000,000 on the other. And the deputation, without going into a general discussion of the tariff, asked one specific thing, and that was that the government should increase the duty on pork from two cents per lb. to four cents per lb. And my hon. friend had not the courage to stand up before the deputation and tell them that he was opposed to their request. I will allow him to interrupt me, if he wishes to do so; I will not be so discourteous to the hon. minister as he was to me in the discussion. I am prepared to say he was afraid of the farmers; he did not have the courage to tell them squarely that he was opposed to it, but sent them home with the thought that possibly they might get the reform they asked for. It will be my business to tell the farmers that the hon.

minister says that the farmers are asking for class legislation, specific legislation in their own interest. And why should they not have protection If we are to have a tariff why should not the farmers have some benefit from it? I may say to my hon. friend that the member for Wentworth read a portion of a resolution from the Swine Breeders' Association and this is a part of it:
While we hesitate to trouble your depart* ment in the matter, we are prompted to do so by the alarming circumstances that there is fifty per cent less hogs produced to-day than there was six months ago, entirely as a result of low prices and the unfair competition, whereas if properly encouraged the resources are quite capable of producing double the quantity of six months ago.
That was the specific statement of these farmers. I may say that the farmers of this country have a right to some consideration. The members of the government, including the hon. gentleman himself, have been playing fast and loose upon this very tariff question. He goes up into the county of Halton and misquotes my hon. friend who represents that county (Mr. Henderson), and tells the farmers that my hon. friend who represents the county is in favour of a Chinese wall upon everything. My hon. friend corrects him now, and he accepts the statement. The minister could have found my hon. friend's statement in the 'Hansard' before he went up to Halton county, if he had wished; but he wanted to misrepresent him I suppose.

I say, Mr. Chairman, that the minister is not frank with the farmers of this country when he allowed a deputation to come before him with a specific request, he is not frank enough to say to them that he is opposed to their request. But he takes the opportunity, in this general discussion, to make the statement that he is not willing to increase the tariff on pork. Now, the minister has stated that I was not ready to divide the House upon the question of the tariff, or rather that I was quite willing, as a representative of the people, from time to time to point out the faults of this government when they did not measure up to the requirements and wishes of the farmers. I am here to say that the minister is well aware that at every session of parliament since I have been a member of it, I have directed the attention of the government to the condition of the farmers. I had the honour of moving more than one resolution calling upon the government to increase the tariff upon the products of market gardens, and my hon. friend and his leader and every member of the government recorded their vote against that motion. They said to the farmers of this country, not only in speech but in vote, that they were opposed to increasing the tariff upon farm products, upon pork, and upon other things wherein the farmers requested a change of tariff. I admit that this is perhaps not an opportune time to bring this matter up. But I am glad I have brought it up, because we have a frank statement from the minister tonight that he is opposed to my request, and the farmers will understand his position and the position of the government. This verv session of parliament I presented, on the floor of this House, the condition of the hog raising industry before the revision of the tariff. If I had left it until after the

revision of the tariff, the minister would have said: 'You should have directed the attention of the government to this matter before the budget was brought down.' We took good care to direct the attention of the minister to this question before the tariff was brought down, and the government had an opportunity to make that correction. The minister, therefore, cannot say to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House that we have not directed the attention of the government to this condition of things. I have no hesitation in saying that the farmers of this country believe that it would be in their interest to get even-handed protection as long as we have a protective tariff. If the time comes when we are able to have a lower tariff the farmers will be prepared to submit, but they are not prepared to submit that the manufacturers of this country and other interests shall have a high protection when they get along -with a reasonable protection upon the articles they produce. To all their arguments the Minister of Agriculture turns a deaf ear, and then goes out upon the hustings and says: 'This government ought to receive the support of the farmers because we are very much interested in their success.' I must congratulate the Minister I suppose if he is in any better humour now, because he has told the House that he is going to expend a sum of money in trying to open up a market, or rather looking into the hog industry in other parts of the world. I suppose he would say this was in the interest of the farmer. Anything that will make the hog raising industry more profitable to the farmer I am in favour of. But I have no hesitation in saying that I am opposed to a tariff that ailows, and did allow last year during six months alone, one million dollars worth of American pork to come into this country under our low tariff, while we have been able to send so little to the United States under the five cent tariff they impose against the Canadian hog products. I tl'ink it is the duty of the Minister of Agriculture to look into this matter, and to see to it that while he is taking care of the manufacturers and others, he pays some attention to the interests of the farmers. I believe that the farmers know their business, and when they come to this government and state that the tariff should be increased from two to four cents a pound, I am one of those who believe that the farmers know what they want, and I am very glad to hear the minister state frankly that he is opposed to the request of the farmers.

Says this Conservative journal:
-that any particular line of industry for which increased protection is demanded is entitled to have its special claims presented, no matter how doubtful a case anybody may beforehand fancy it to have; but when at this era a proclamation is heard such as Mr. Biain of Peel uttered, that there should be a tariff high enough to keep out of Canada every dollar's worth of goods that we can produce, one is prompted to express some amazement. Mr. Biain is a Conservative. If the party were to father his views, we fancy that it would injure itself seriously, indeed probably remain out of power indefinitely in Canada. We doubt if there was ever a time when a country in which such a doctrine was or could be very sensible; and the present time, when in the home and citadel of high protection, namely, tho United States, there is a popular revolt which is forcing the protectionist and ruling party to scale down the tariff, would, we imagine, be . a peculiarly inopportune time for the Conservative party in Canada to allow itself to go further than it has in the direction of high tariff.
I would not feel justified in delaying the committee to read the whole article, but if any hon. gentleman wishes to read what this important Conservative journal says upon this subject, I shall be glad to send him over the paper.
