Canada could produce (i.e., manufacture) numberless things, to attempt to produce which would be folly. If this country were to adopt such a dictum as Mr. Biaim's, that we should keep out every dollar's worth of goods that we can produce, we would keep out great quantities of manufactures which could certainly be produced in Canada, but only at such a comparatively high cost that if our people were compelled to pay the proportionate retail prices, the expense of private living here would be desperately increased. We imagine that the people of Canada would refuse to have this sort of thing fastened upon them to any greater degree than at present. At any rate, whatever might be argued as to the possibility of such a doctrine being tolerated in eastern Canada, there is no chance of the new western Canada putting up with it; and. so from merely a party point of view, if the Conservative party hopes for any gain in the prairie provinces-where it needs to Mr. FIELDING
gain if it is to succeed-the less said about high protectionism the better. Canada has a tariff more than high enough to contribute efficiently towards national solidarity, a tariff high enough to give ample protection to every Canadian industry which has a fair excuse for existence; a tariff apparently well calculated to produce as large a revenue as our governments need to be entrusted with. We fancy, then, that it is a good tariff to let alone, except to cut down where undue business combines are shown to be sheltered by it.
That is the declaration of a Conservative journal in this Dominion of Canada. That is the declaration of the Ottawa 'Evening Journal.' Will some one say that it is a mere individual opinion? The Ottawa 'Evening Journal' is published by a gentleman who was a candidate for the Conservative party in the city of Ottawa and the night before that article was published he was chosen to be president of the Conservative association of Ottawa. So, they bid farewell to adequate protection.

I need not go on with the list, I think I have given sufficient to show how this tariff encourages importation instead of encouraging production. Under the Conservative policy of promoting production on the farm and in the factory, people got articles at a reasonable price, but under this new policy of promoting importation in order to get revenue, you see the prices we have to pay. Possibly we get goods at a lower rate of duty; but what signifies that if we have to pay thirty or forty or fifty per cent more on the cost of the goods? I do not regard it as of moment that we are able to fill the treasury with money to build municipal bridges or wharfs where there is no water, or to do a great many other things that are not called for in the country, if you are taking it out of the pockets of the people by compelling them to pay a higher price for what they consume. Now, I think I have made the Minister of Finance thoroughly to understand my position on the tariff. I am a moderate protectionist. I do not believe in raising the tariff simply to get revenue. Readjustment is what we want. If I had my way, I would put the duty on agricultural implements down to 10 per cent. I would say to the men who are manufacturing reapers and mowers: 'If you do not put the price down ten per cent below what it was last year. I will bring down the duty.' If they will not reduce the price, I say reduce the duty. But if they will reduce the price, I am not so unpatriotic as to say that these things should not be made in Canada. The government should use the tariff as a power to regulate the prices of manufactured articles. My hon. friend, the Finance Minister, has told us that the people of the Northwest want a low tariff. Why then does he not lower the duty on agricultural implements to 10 per cent? The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) told us the other day that the government had reduced the duty on ploughs and some other agricultural implements to 174 per cent. I am sure that was a surprise to the Finance Minister as it was to me. I hope the hon. member for South Grey did not intend that speech to go to the Northwest. The only two articles on which the duties were reduced to 174 per cent were mowers and binders. If the minister wants to do something for the west-and I do not believe that the people there are free traders, I do not believe that even my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) would want absolutely no duties at all, I believe the people there are willing to pay their fair share to the revenues of the country-but there are certain lines on which they want the duties reduced. Take agricultural implements, I will say put the duty on these heavy implements that cost a lot of money

and which the farmers must have, down to a lower figure. I think the manufacturer can stand it, especially on the larger implements such as binders and mowers, because they are large exporters and do not rely on the home trade. They have an enormous foreign trade, and if their home trade were wiped out they could live on their foreign trade.

speechtext:
Just a moment while I am on my feet; I do not wish tc delay the estimates. I think we had better come back to a few of these agricultural items. Hon. members opposite are continually making believe that there is a difference between the manufacturer and the farmer. To my mind, the farmer is the largest manufacturer in the country. He employs more labour than any body,else, he pays more for his tools and uses more tools than other producers do, and he works harder than the man of any other class. If there is any one who should be protected, to my mind it is the farmer, for he produces fully 65 per cent of the products of this country. Now, I call the attention of Iron, gentlemen to a few figures -and I will permit the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the Minister of Agriculture also (Mr. Fisher) to sleep on the rtems that I have to bring forward. I took occasion to go through the Trade and Commerce returns to ascertain the amount of goods imported into this country that mrght be raised and should be raised on the farms of this country. In the first place, I find- that of farm animals we imported $1 649,574 worth.	Of breadstuffs,
our imports amounted to $16,524,968-and we proclaim ourselves a great country fof the production of breadstuffs, and the government takes credit for being good to the people of the Northwest whose chief product is breadstuffs. Of green fruits our imports were $5,312,798.	The green-fruit
growers claim that they are not protected but are under unfair competition from the growers in the United States who can get into the market here earlier in the season than we can. In gloves and mitts, which our mothers and grandmothers used to make years ago, _we imported $2,987,556. Of axle grease which used to be a common article manufactured in this country-we imported last year $878,268 worth. Hides are a product of the animals grown on the farms of Canada, and one would think that we could produce our own hides. But on the contrary, we find that we imported last year $4,908,871 worth of hides. And Mr. J. A. CURRIE.
still we pride ourselves in being a great cattle-growing country, and speak of ourselves as doing everything to protect the farming interest of our country. Of honey our imports last year amounted to $35,405. Hops-something our farmers grow in Kent county and all through the western part of the Ontario peninsula-used to be exported from this country. Last year, we imported $235,923 worth. Turn again to the leathers and manufactures thereof; one would think that when we import the hides we would surely make the leather, but we find that we imported of these goods $3,780,303 worth. Milk, that surely is the product of this country yet we find that last year we imported $199,624 worth. Then we come to plants and trees - we have nurseries of our own, and yet we bring in $276,683 worth. Our imports of provisions, such as butter, cheese and articles of that description amount to no less than $4,655,980. ^ And still we are told the farmer is not in need of protection. Of seeds and roots-and these articles surely should be produced in this country-we imported $4,. 559,454 worth. And now I come to the item of sugar. Hon. gentlemen opposite have claimed that they have endeavoured to stimulate the sugar industry, and surely all must agree that the sugar industry should be successful in this country. One or two factories have been successful, but owing to some cause, whether the lack of proper protection or not, a large number of these factories have gone out of business. The result is that instead of producing our own sugar, as is done in Germany and France under virtually similar conditions of climate and soil, we imported last year $12,433,111 worth. Then we c-ome to tobacco. The hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) has an item in his estimates for the encouragment of the growth of tobacco in this country. The tobacco industry is certainly a growing industry and the to-baeco growers of Canada have shown clearly that they can produce as good tobacco as can be produced anywhere in the world. In spite of that, instead of protecting the tobacco industry of western Ontario, we imported last year $4,356,820 worth of tobacco.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentle man (Mr. J. A. Currie) wish a higher duty on tobacco?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I think that some method should be adopted to encourage the growing of tobacco in this country. I feel satisfied that, if the tobacco industry of this country is properly encouraged, within a very few years, instead of merely producing our own supply of tobacco, we shall become an exporting country. If the hon. minister (Mr. Fielding) will turn up the returns of this country back in the forties

and fifties, he will find that in those days Canada exported tobacco. But he will not go back that far. The next item I have here is that of green vegetables, representing an industry in whose success my hon. friend from Centre York (Mr. Wallace) has shown a deep interest. Last year, we imported $1,117,253 worth of green vegetables. The last item is an article that we on this side are all agreed should be produced in this country-woollens. Last year, our im ports of woollens amounted to no less than $23,145,029. Certainly, a very large proportion of these goods should be produced in this country. Now, how much is represented altogether by these imports of goods that might be produced on Canadian farms? Last year, the Northwest produced wheat to the value of perhaps $80 000,000. Yet we find that articles imported into this country in direct competition with the product of out farms represented a value of no less than $87,157,628.
Now, the hon. minister (Mr. Fielding), I suppose, has such a fine, keen, acute mind that he would try to put questions to. me to show that I must be either a protectionist or a free trader or nothing. I can tell the hon. minister that I find that his party is in practically the same shape as they were in 1878, when Alexander Mackenzie was defeated. At that time, their policy was one of tariff for revenue only, which is the policy they claim to have now. The question of tariff for revenue only was never fought out on the platform in this country except in 1878, and then it was swamped so badly that it is only of recent years we have heard anything more about it. The hon. minister knows that Sir John Macdonald pointed out that the policy of tariff for revenue only was one which put upon the farmer and the artisan the greatest amount of taxation. Sir John Macdonald introduced his national policy in opposition to the policy of Alexander Mackenzie. It was not a policy of high protection, but of adjustment of the taxation so as to increase the industries suited to the country, while taking a minimum of taxes out of the pockets of the people. I would recommend the hon. member for Bed Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) to read the speeches in the campaign of 1878. He will find there a great distinction between free trade and tariff for revenue only, and a great distinction also between the national policy and the policy of high protection. I do not think any Conservative can stand up and defend the policy of high protection. We are said to be high protectionists. I have always understood that protection, as advocated by Sir John Macdonald and ,the Conservative party to be in the truest sense a national policy for this country. Now, what is it that causes trouble to the
farmers with regard to the sale of their products? The market was all right when they had good times in the United States, and they could find a high market for their products. But hon. gentlemen know that within the last two or three years there have been hard times in the United States, and the farmers there have had difficulty in selling their products, and the result is that their .surplus is shipped into this country at a lower price than our farmers were getting, and our farmers must take a lower price. I think the discussion perhaps has gone a little further afield than it .should. But so far as I am concerned,
I believe that the welfare of this country lies in a proper system of protection for the articles the farmers produce.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The discussion has been very broad. I have no desire to stop it if the committee really desires to engage in a discussion of tariff issues; but I think I should remind the committee that the item is that for the development of the live stock industry.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I am perfectly sure, Mr. Chairman, that you as well as the committee will have no reason to complain of the length of any observations I address to the House, because I have from the beginning of this discussion had exactly the view you have expressed, that our opinions upon the tariff would have been better expressed in the budget debate. I did take what I hoped was a pardonable liberty in asking my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) if I might introduce him to his leader's definition of adequate protection in the debates of 1902. With his usual courtesy he granted me leave to give his leader's definition. I have the definition which I gave here, and I think the House will corroborate what I noted down immediately, and it is substantially what I said:	' A
tariff against the United States at least as high as that of the United States against us.' Now the hon. member for Halton is not only very courteous, but he is a somewhat wily old member of this House, and he had far too much sense to contradict me, because he knew I was perfectly correct. He had this advantage over the member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples), that he had a better memory of what his leader had said; so he did not expose himself in the way that the member for Macdonald did. Some other members gave the member for Macdonald their moral support by asserting- referring to the leader of the opposition- ' He never said it.' I have in my hands now the ' Hansard ' of 1902, and I will read from the speech of the leader of the opposition what he said in that debate, as found on page 1334 in volume 1;
One would expect that if we intend to maintain and build up our own products and manu-

factures against such powerful and tremendous competition as that which we must anticipate from the United States, we would fix our tariff of customs against that country on a scale at least as high as is that of their tariff against us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asked my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) if he would accept the defini-ition of adequate protection as given by his leader, and my hon. friend from Halton answered that he would, and I said that the leader of the opposition never did make any such definition of adequate protection. I say still that he never made any such definition, and I challenge the hon. gentleman to read from ' Hansard ' the context in that speech, and he cannot find that the leader of the opposition defined adequate protection in the terms he has used.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: If I am not wearying the patience of the House, I will take up the point as it has been raised by my hon. friend from Macdonald. The speech from which I am quoting

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. This discussion has no reference at all to the item before the Chair. I think we ought to adhere to the item under discussion. We have wandered far away from the item, and I ask that we now come back to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The point of order raised by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) is certainly well taken. The discussion for the last hour has been almost entirely out of order. I have not felt called upon to insist on the rule, because it appeared to be the desire of the committee to discuss the tariff generally. But now that the point of order has been raised, I must rule that the committee come back to the discussion of the item for the development of the live stock industry.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) was within his right when he sought to show the Minister of Agriculture the necessity of making some improvement in the hog industry, in view of the manner in which it is languishing at present. I feel it is my duty to call upon the Minister of Agriculture to take immediate steps to improve the position of that industry. If lie will examine the agricultural press he will find that he is being severely condemned for the manner in which that industry is languishing. In turning up the trade and navigation returns I find that last year 11,770,000 pounds of lard, valued at $1,000,000, came into this country. Of bacon, ham, shoulders and sides, 7, 304,000 pounds, valued at $851,000, came in from the United States. Of pork, barreled in brine, 9,204,000 pounds, valued at $713,000, came in. Surely my hon. friend

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: from Peel was within his rights in calling the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the position of the swine industry. In view of the fact that in the neighbourhood of 30,000,000 pounds of swine products are annually coming into this country, surely my hon. friend was within his rights in calling the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the fact that the swine indus try was not increasing, but that it was an industry that was in need of a radical change. The Minister of Agriculture tells us that he is going to send a few farmers over to Denmark to see if they can bring back some new ideas. If these men return within the next few months it will take years for the swine industry to get back to anything like the position it held some years ago. Let him look at the pork manufactories in Canada and see the small amount of pork that is being exported and he cannot help but come to the conclusion that his department is responsible for the position of the swine industry to-day. When you take into consideration the very large imports of that product from the United States and other countries you cannot help but come to the conclusion that the minister has been neglecting that industry. He may look at the butter industry and the man who is at the head of the dairy department in the country may tell the people just as much as he likes that we are producing just about the same quantity as we ever did, he can say that it is because of the increase of population, or he can offer other excuses along these lines, but the fact remains that instead of these products having largely increased as they have in other countries, the increase has been very much less. Let the minister go to New Zealand and see the wonderful de-velopements in production and increase in exports that have taken place there. Let him go to the Argentine Republic and see what they are doing in the live stock industry there. If he compares the exports of these countries with our exports he cannot help but feel humiliated, as every Canadian does in this agricultural country, at the lack of advancement in the development of this live stock industry. I do not wish to take up the time of the House-

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knowles) says ' hear, hear.1 If the hon. member for Assiniboia would take a little more interest in the development of the farm industry of our great west than he does in this House, instead of yelling ' hear, hear,' when he knows full well that the Minister of Agriculture has been neglecting his duty in regard to these important subjects, he would be doing something for the general benefit of the people of his province.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. I have listened painfully to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) many times in this House, and I have never thought that the Minister of Agriculture has neglected any of his duties.
Mr. DEPUTY, SPEAKER. There is no question of privilege in the remarks which the hon. gentleman has made.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is naturally interested in his constituency, and after the remarks we have listened to I do not know that I will attempt to make any reply. When I call attention to the fact that we are making these large importations of the products of the farm, I cannot help but feel that something should be done, and done immediately, whereby our farm products could be increased and whereby the swine industry, the butter industry and the live stock industry could be developed along more extensive lines than at the present time. I feel that if the minister would take into consideration not only the question of developing the swine, the butter and the live stock industries of this country, but the question of securing the best possible markets for the products of the farm, he would be doing a greater measure of justice to the farmers of this country than he is doing at the present time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I desire just to say a few words in reference to the question of the development of our live stock industry When I take up the trade figures issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce it seems to me as if the money expended for the development of the live stock industry during the last couple of years has not produced results such as we could desire. We see that the export of live cattle in the year 1906 was about $2,000,000 greater than in the year 1908, showing that we are falling back to a very great extent in the development of our cattle industry. While the numbei of cattle exported was 25,000 less, the number of horses was several hundred less and the value very much reduced. The export of sheep was just about the same. In the products of the hog-ham and bacon-we have fallen back about a million dollars. It appears to me that the money which has been expended in the past couple of years has not had the desired effect in developing our live stock industry. How does the Minister of Agriculture account for this great falling off in our exportation of live stock? It is true that our population is a little greater than it was two years ago and no doubt consumes more, but still the increase in the production of stock and animal products should be greater than the increase of population. Parliament has voted a con siderable amount every year for the develop ment of the live stock industry. We are
willing to vote for that purpose, provided we can obtain good results, a still larger sum. But, when we see that the results are not satisfactory and that our country is going backward in regard to its live stock industry, it seems to me that something should be done to improve this condition. I would ask the minister how he explains the falling off in the exportation of live stock?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Unfortunately we have not complete statistics year by year of home consumption or of the number of animals in the country. I have no doubt whatever that the falling off in the export of horses is due to the increased demand in this country to supply the needs of the new settlers in the Northwest. I do not understand the exact reason for the falling off in the export of cattle, but the decrease in the export of dairy products in the last few seasons would doubtless be due to the diminished production of milk on account of the drought; the decreased production of Canadian butter not keeping pace with the relatively increased consumption at home. The dry season has also affected the hog industry very seriously. It is largely dependent upon the dairy industry, and when dairying is short the cost of producing pork and its products increases. The price of grain and feed stuffs during the last few years has been exceptiohally high, with the result that our farmers have been discouraged in rearing hogs. Although the price of pork has been rather high, and very high lately, th_e farmers say that the margin of profit between the cost of production and the price to them was not sufficient to encourage them to increase production. It is for the purpose of finding out whether there are methods of production in Denmark and Ireland which are more economical than our own that I propose to send this commission to these countries. If we can get any hints which will help our industry it will he well worth the expenditure. I would prefer to send farmers who themselves are engaged in the industry rather than officers of my department, whose reports might be criticised and might perhaps not be considered so acceptable.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The falling off in the export of butter is really astonishing. In 1907 about $7,000,000 worth of butter was exported and in 1908 only $1,000,000 worth, showing a falling off of $6,000,000 in one year. The inference might possibly be that the farmers were making cheese instead of butter, but there is a falling off in the export of cheese to the extent of $2,000,000 worth. All along the line of the live stock and dairying industry there seems to have been an immense falling off during the past year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I was sorry to hear the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture with regard to the Alaska-Yukon-Seattle exposition. It would seem strange if the stock raisers of the west do not themselves know what is for their own interest in that respect. I have the very strongest requests from the executive officers of the association representing the three western provinces asking for some small assistance to enable them to exhibit their live stock at Seattle. But the minister positively Refused to entertain that request. I should have thought that these gentlemen must have taken into consideration the difficulty regarding the quarantine and that they believed this difficulty could be overcome. The western breeders have invested very large sums of money to improve the breed of horses and cattle; and as we do a considerable trade with that part of the United States the Seattle exhibition would be a grand opportunity to show what western Canadian farmers have succeeded in accomplishing. About $8,000 is all that these gentlemen ask; it is a small sum for such a worthy object, and I have had numerous letters and 'telegrams from them asking me to urge the minister to give this aid.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The returns which have reached me have come from Mr. Bell of Winnipeg, representing as I understand the Western Farmers' Association. The hon. gentleman is more fortunate than I am with regard to receiving letters and telegrams of that kind.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I have received copies of resolutions from the farmers' associations in Saskatchewan, which I understood had been sent to the Minister of Agriculture.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I think the only communication I have received was from Manitoba.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I would remind the minister that a number of British Columbia breeders exhibited at the Portland exhibition a few years ago and did very well indeed. Are the quarantine conditions more onerous now than they were then?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I would recall the attention of the minister to an application from a resident in my district, Mr. Page of Matsqui which engaged the attention of this House on a former occasion. I understood the Minister of Agriculture to say then that Mr. Page had a claim; perhaps not a legal claim, but sufficient of a claim to warrant the government in giving consideration to it, and .this led Mr. Page to hope that at some time or other he might get compensation from the government. The facts of the case are:	Mr. Page was a

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: breeder of horses and he sent quite a large consignment to the United States, feeling that the regulations then in force permitted him to have them entered free of duty as they were imported to be sold for breeding purposes. The customs officers of the United States told him his interpretation of their law was wrong, and, as he had irregularly imported these horses into the United States they were seized and confiscated and sold, resulting in the loss to Mr. Page of the entire shipment. Mr. Page then made a claim to the Department of Agriculture, stating that his exportation was under the terms agreed upon between the two countries and as understood by the Canadian department, and being led into error by accepting the Canadian interpretation of the American regulations his claim comes before the department as a matter of compassion, or perhaps I should say of common justice. I undrstood the minister to say on the occasion I have referred to that he was disposed to do something for Mr. Page. Does the hon. gentleman consider that incident entirely closed, or is it possible that something may yet be done?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I have considered the incident entirely closed for some years. The question is not a question of any action on the part of this government. The action was taken by the American authorities, and we have no control over their interpretation of their own law. The actual fact was this: Under the American regulations horses imported for breeding purposes are free of duty. This gentleman brought horses into the United States to sell, and the American authorities interpreted the regulations to mean that that was not bringing them in for breeding purposes. This government have nothing whatever to do with the action of the American authorities, and I never understood that Mr. Page expected or asked for compensation from this government. I think he asked that we should deal with the American, authorities, and we did so. We represented' to the Secretary of State at Washington that it was a case of hardship, and asked that it should be reconsidered. It was reconsidered and discussed at headquarters at Washington, and I think it was the Attorney General of the United States who declared that the interpretation put upon the American regulations by the officers at the frontier, was a legal and proper interpretation. I do not see how we could possibly have done anything more than we did, and I cannot understand how Mr. Page or any body else could claim that the government of Canada could be held responsible for such an action.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
My recollection is that the hon. minister said something

which led Mr. Page to believe that this government would do something for him. I have had a letter from him asking me to mention the matter again.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I cannot remember any words of mine that could be so interpreted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Has the hon. minister before him the request in writing that was made by the Swinebreeders' Association?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: No, I haven't it here.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Did my hon. friend say that it referred to anything except the unfair competition found in the Canadian market?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I cannot say that the writing did, but the deputation that came to me made a request for this commission. My hon. friend accused me a few minutes ago of lack of courage in not telling the 6winebreeders what I have told the House to-night. My hon. friend ought to know that the government always refuses to say to any deputation what they are going to do with regard to tariff matters.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Do I understand that another deputation waited on the hon. gentleman, but that it had no reference to the tariff?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Certain swine breeders approached my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and mv hon. friend the Minister of Customs, as well as myself, in regard to the tariff. Then a deputation of swine-breeders came to me in my office and asked for this commission. I am inclined to think that they were largely the same men. I can remember some of them-Mr. Breth-our, Mr. Featherstone and Mr. Flatt-and there were several members of parliament with them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Are these the men to be sent over?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: No. They said they did not wish swine-breeders to be sent; they preferred that swine feeders should be sent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Is there not some way in which the minister could make better progress than by sending over a commission? It appears to me that it is not a bad suggestion in itself, but it will be many months before this commission will be able to make a report, and a still longer time before the people will be educated up to their ideas. Could not the minister take some more aggressive course to remedy this state of affairs?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: We have always acted on the line of educating the farmers, impressing upon them what has been found by experiment to be the best method of fattening hogs. That, of course, does not affect the price of the hog or the cost of the feed. All we can do is to explain the relative values of different feeds, and leave them to find the best feed, and feed it in the cheapest way possible. We propose to continue that work of education, and I hope it will have some effect. In the past it has had a very great effect. But largely because feed has been scarce and high lately, the profits on hog feeding have not been as great as they were a few years ago. During the last two years the price of hogs sold on the Canadian market has been usually high. It is always the case in the fall of the year that the price of hogs goes down; but I may say that the average price during the last two years has been higher than it was in the two yeaTS before.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: One reason to mv mind why the farmers are going out of the raising of hogs is the very unstable condition of the market. The minister knows well that it is very irregular. At one time of the year there is a price that will perhaps make the raising of hogs profitable. The fall of the year, when the bulk of the hogs are marketed, and when the farmer expects to receive his profit, is the time when the price is very low. There is a general impression in the part of the country that I come from that the packers have an organization, and at a time of the year when they are about to put in their supplies for home consumption, they put the price down. I would like to ask the minister if he does not think that if the Canadian farmer had the home market for himself, it would help to regulate the price to a considerable extent. I am not going to advocate high protection, but I do believe in fair trade; and if my neighbours charge us five cents a pound to get an article into their country, I think we would be justified, to a certain extent anyway, in protecting our own industries. How'ever, wre have not time to discuss that question now, but I cannot agree with the minister that such a policy would raise the price to the consumer. He said he was very pleased to belong to the agricultural class. I agree with him, as I am a farmer myself. He also said that the farmers were very charitable and did not ask for a tariff which would raise the prices to the masses. I quite agree that they are' charitable or they would not have supported this government so long in return for. so little; but the farmers in the riding I represent believe in protecting their own market to the extent, or very nearly so, asked by the Swine Breeders' Association. Does the hon. minister not think it would be well to look into the matter from the packers' standpoint so as to ascertain, whether the general belief be true that they combine to unduly press the prices down, especially in September and October?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I did have an investigation made into the comparative prices _ of the live hog at the station to the packing houses and the wholesale price of the finished products in the shape of bacons and hams and the retail price tqjhe consumer. What I had done was to compare the prices in these different articles in Chicago, Buffalo, Toronto, Montreal and Liverpool over a period covering six months. We took the prices as we found them reported in the Trade journals every week, beginning in September or October, 1907 and during the six months following. The result showed that if we took the price paid for the live hog at the station and made reasonable allowance for the cost of manufacture, transport, &c., .the price received for Canadian bacon on the Liverpool market, wholesale, delivered there, was not an undue profit over the price paid the farmer. But if you take the price paid by the Canadian consumer in Montreal or Toronto for the'finished bacon over the counter, it was much laTger on that portion of the hog sold in Canada than on the portion sold in England. In other words, the retail price in Canada showed a profit much larger than the retail price in England. As far as our investigation went, the figures would indicate that the increase lay between the departure of the pork from the factory and its sale by the retailer, but just how it was distributed we had no means of finding out. My impression, from that investigation, is that if to-day the packers are making very large profits, they are doing that on the retail sale in the Canadian market and not on their sale in the English market. The price paid to the Canadian farmer at the station for the live hog seemed to be as high as the packer could pay and make a fair profit on his business when he sold at the prices in the English market. That investigation took place a year ago, and I have not had time to have it repeated, but I will see that it is repeated this coming season and find out more information for the benefit of the farmers and the trade.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Is the hon. minister aware that thousands of cattle are slaughtered in this country every year, affected with tuberculosis and sold to the people? I have had several complaints recently.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I am not aware that thousands of cattle affected with tuberculosis have been sold in the country. In the meat establishments, which are under the control of my department since the Meat and Canned Food Act has been passed, here are no carcasses affected with tuberculosis which are allowed to pass through and enter into consumption. There is a small percentage of the cattle slaughtered in those establishments found Mr. SEXSMITH.
affected with tuberculosis, but I would be sorry to admit for a moment, in the general way my hon. friend uses the term, that there are thousands of cattle slaughtered in Canada which are thus affected.
To encourage the production and use of superior seeds of farm crops and for the enforcement of the Seed Control Act, $49,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: There is a reduction here of $19,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: That is due to the transfer of the salaries to the civil government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Is the hon. minister distributing seed at present?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The only distribution is in small packages by post from the Experimental farm.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: How is it proposed to expend the money?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: There are salaries to officers outside of Ottawa amounting to $7,500. There is a very considerable amount of travel of the staffs, which costs about $8,000. The printing and stationery take $6,000. The book called ' The Farm Weeds of Canada ' will call for an expenditure from this year's appropriation of $6,000. Part of the expense of the new edition has already been paid out of this year's vote. We also-propose to issue a publication on grasses, clovers and forage crops, which is expected to cost $6,000. Supplies for the laboratory will cost $1,250, and supplies for the Calgary laboratory $750. The expense of enforcing the Seed Control Act, apart from the salaries of officers, is $2,000. Then, we assist in conducting seed fairs and field competitions in the growth of seed grain, and assist the associations. This costs $12,000. There is a special grant to the Canadian Seed Growers' Association and Provincial Seed Exhibition of $5,500.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: You have lecturers going about?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Yes, that is included in the salaries. They also assist in enforcing the Seed Control Act.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Are the farmers still permitted to sell seed grain without inspection? I know from inquiry among some of the men dealing in seeds that they doubt veTy much whether this Act can be made very successful so long as the farmers are permitted to sell to their neighbours seed grain that is not inspected. x\s I understand it, the inspection reaches only the dealers, but one of the great sources of trouble in the distribution of foul seed is the farmers selling seed grain to one another.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
The Seed Control Act has a provision under which a farmer growing seed can sell it to his neighbours. That

was discussed when the Seed Control Act was passed, and there has been no amendment to that section; the law remains as it has been for some years. My hon. friend (Mr. Lalor) was here, I think, when the Act was passed, and knows the reasons why the provision was put in. I need not dwell upon them now.
To encourage the production and sale of Canadian tobacco, $5,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I was glad to hear an hon. member say that we ought to encourage the tobacco growing industry of this country. He will approve a vote for that purpose. I have been doing a little work in this way for some time back, and this year hope to do still more. What I did before was not under a special vote, but under the general encouragement of markets and agricultural products of 'the country. But this year, expecting to do more, I am asking for a special vote. The work we have been doing has been to give instruction to the tobacco growers and to carry on experiments especially in the curing of the tobacco. I think there is no doubt that Canada can produce a very large quantity of tobacco. The soil is suitable, and the climate seems _ to be suitable. But the curing and handling by the farmers has been deficient. We are trying to help them in this matter. In the coming season I propose, partly through this vote-but there will have to be a vote for special buildings-to establish three experimental stations, one in Essex county, Ontario, one in Montcalm, and one in Rou-ville, in Quebec, these latter two very small ones not costing as much as the single one in Essex, to carry on experiments in the way of growing tobacco and some new kinds, and especially in the curing of the tobacco in accordance with the experiments we have been conducting, and also with the experiments in handling that have been carried on in the United States.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Is there to be any expenditure for the encouragement of tobacco growing in British Columbia?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I was not proposing to establish an experimental station in British Columbia this year. My tobacco expert has not been able yet to study the conditions in British Columbia and work out what is the right thing to do, but I propose to have him go there and study the situation, and if we can do anything in the way of experimental work there we shall be glad to undertake it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I am glad the minister has decided to establish an experimental station in the western peninsula. I know the need of it there, and I hope he will give it his energetic attention.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
How does the minister make his statement correspond with the state-186
ment in opposition to the manufacture of cigarettes in this country?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
If they would use no tobacco in Canada but export it all, I should be glad. I do not use it myself, and should like to see others follow my example. But if they are going to use tobacco, I would like to see them use good tobacco.
Contributions towards maintenance of and expenses of representation at International Institute of Agriculture, $10,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I suppose I should give an explantion of this.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: A short one.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I will try to be short. I have this to say to my hon. friend, however -I sympathize with his desire to put these items through as quickly as possible, but he must not expect that his friends are to be allowed to say just what they wish' and we to say nothing. This International Institute of Agriculture was finally established in Rome last year, the initiative having been taken in 1905, when the representatives of the great powers in Europe and America practically joined and decided to establish it. It seemed to me-and on investigating I am confirmed in the opinion -that this is an institute which may be productive of the greatest good in the agricultural world. It is an organization of an international character foT the purpose of collecting statistics and other information and distributing it. It is practically a clearing house of agricultural information. And, although we in Canada sometimes plume ourselves on the advanced state of our agriculture, and -our experimental progress in all agricultural subjects-I confess that I pride myself on that as a Canadian -there is no doubt that we can learn from other countries, and we can learn very much from the older countries of Europe and Asia, as well as from the newer countries of America. This institute is for the purpose of collecting information from all these countries and placing it at the disposal of the members. On the invitation of the authorities, we agreed to adhere, first in a modest wav in what is called the fourth class. But when I came to examine the matter, I found that that was hardly commensurate with what I believed to be the importance of Canada as an agricultural country and the importance of our agricultural interest, and so asked that Canada be raised to the second class, where we have to pay a somewhat larger contribution toward the expenses of the institute. Another thing we have to do is to have an officer or representative of the country in the management of the institute. I was fortunate enough, last fall, when I went to represent this government, to be able to secure the services of a gen-

tleman from Montreal, Mr. Arthur Boyer, well known in the public life of Quebec, a gentleman who has lived in the city, but is familiar also with the agricultural conditions and the country life of Canada. He was also familiar with the French language, and a gentleman of high character and great intelligence. So well were we represented at the meeting in Rome last November, that the Hon. Mr. Boyer was chosen one of a small executive committee of five to manage the affairs of the institute. We have also to prepare and send to the institute agricultural and statistical information from our own country in order that it may be tabulated along with such information from other countries and I am asking for $10,000 for the purpose of doing this work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: How is that information to be made available to the farmers?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
The Department of Agriculture will get the information and distribute it. The information, however, will probably be of a character rather suitable for students and the scientific farmer, than the ordinary farmer. But we hope to be able to distribute to the farmers abstracts of the statistics. A farmer who wants this information can send to the department and get it. This institute at Rome will secure information from all countries in the world with regard to any new process that it may be desirable to introduce, or any new discovery that may be made of importance to agriculture generally.
Steamers to replace 'Argus' and 'Challenger, $40,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: These are vessels required for the quarantine service and have been so long in use that they are now almost unsafe, and our engineers report that they must be replaced.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: What has the 'Challenger' been doing?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The 'Challenger' is one of the boats at the Grosse Isle station in Quebec, the 'Argus' is stationed at Halifax.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman expect it will cost to put a boat on the quarantine station at Halifax to replace the 'Argus'? I understood the minister to say that that boat was about to be condemned. As a matter of fact that boat has not been in use for over a year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: She has been under repairs.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: I think she has been out of commission altogether for over a year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: She has been somewhat rut of repair, and not working.

speechtext: For how manv months?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Perhaps six months.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The crew of that boat has been doing nothing all that time. If the minister intends to put a boat on that service that will be equal to the requirements at Halifax, I do not think that he can possibly do it with $10,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: If I find I cannot do it with this vote I will have to ask for more m a supplementary vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
Last year the hon. gentleman had $30,000, and this year he is asking for $40,000.
.iMr- FISHER. We were not able to use the $30,000 and it lapsed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Before the end of the last fiscal year we advertised for a boat to be purchased. A large number of boats were presented to the commission appointed to examine them, and the commission condemned them all. They were of all prices, ot all sizes and of all shapes, and none were satisfactory to the commission. The commission was composed of an officer from the quarantine staff, one from the Marine Department and one from the Public Works Department, all experts. Not having been able to buy a boat, plans and specifications are now in course of preparation for the purpose of getting a boat built, I think before long or before next fall we will succeed in having a boat.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: Surely the statement that the hon. member for Halifax makes that the minister has kept a crew under pay a whole year doing nothing and no boat on which to employ them is not correct?

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext: The crew have other work at the station which they have been doing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-HON. WM. PUGSLEY AND THE REPORT OF THE CENTRAL RAILWAY COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I would rather have the crew kept idle for a year than have a boat put upon this service that is not suitable.
I am glad to hear that the minister has made efforts in the direction he has indicated. If the hon. gentleman finds it impossible to get a boat already constructed, and I imagine that he will find it difficult to do that, it would be really better to build a boat for that service, and I hope that this will be done as speedily as possible.
